# How the code is put together

The sources are listed in `README.md` and `APPENDIX_A_model.md`. This file
covers the code: what goes where, and the decisions behind it. It's updated
every time a decision is made, so it's always the current picture. Where a
later decision changed an earlier one, the earlier one says so.

## Folder layout

Three layers, each one unaware of the ones above it:

- `src/` is the core: models, controllers, runs. No GUI, and no plotting except
  the shared `plotting.py`.
- `workbench/presenter.py` is the GUI's interaction logic, with no Qt in it.
- `workbench/view.py` and `panels.py` are the PyQt shell.

The command line (`src/cli.py`) and the numbered scripts in `notebooks/` call
the core directly.

```text
sx-cascade-control/
  ARCHITECTURE.md       this file
  PROGRESS.md           build log, newest first
  README.md, REPORT.md, APPENDIX_*.md   the write-up
  configs/              one TOML run file per circuit: stages, cut, feed, flows, scrub,
                        strip, saponification, targets, [plant] (which plant to drive)
  params/
    parameters.toml     every number, labelled measured / chosen / derived; [targets]
                        (spec, recovery, design purity) and [design] (net product,
                        pump ceiling and headroom, organic minimum)
    feeds.toml          Carester Table 1, verbatim
    edits_sized_stages.toml  stages sized to the design flows (decision 28), as edits
  src/                  THE CORE
    params.py           the parameter file as Params (from the file or an edited dict)
    config.py           a run file, checked, defaults filled, edits written in
                        (including a run file's own [parameter_edits])
    chemistry.py        distribution coefficients, densities
    circuit.py          the connection map and the circuit's equations (CasADi)
    simulate.py         integration, steady states, implicit Euler for model states
    commission.py       start-up on the design handles; the trim under control
    design.py           operating point by optimization (IPOPT on the steady state)
    mismatch.py         the perturbed plant's numbers, from a seed
    plant_models.py     plants built differently from the model: settler, entrainment
    disturbances.py     the upset types; scenarios.py: the catalogue of eight, explained
    sensors.py          instruments: kind, stage, noise, delay, interval
    estimator.py        state estimate from the readings, with disturbance states
    mpc.py              the controller (measure, bias, linearize, predict, solve, advance)
    loop.py             plant + controller + scenario, stepped one interval at a time
    metrics.py          purity, recovery, losses, interfaces, reagent, transition cost
    registry.py         the named plants, controllers and sensor sets, each explained
    operating_point.py  commission + trim, the start of every study
    runs.py             RunSpec -> session -> result -> saved folder; the one entry point
    cli.py              list / run / matrix from the command line
    plotting.py         the report figures' look (matplotlib)
    rl_env.py           the gymnasium environment for the learned policy
    mpc_nonlinear.py    the do-mpc attempt, kept as a record (too slow)
  workbench/            THE GUI (python -m workbench)
    presenter.py        interaction logic and the WorkbenchView interface; no Qt
    view.py             the PyQt window: every panel a dock, layout remembered
    panels.py           the passive panels: run choices, settings tree, circuit
                        drawing, live plots, stage profile, scorecard, saved runs
  notebooks/            numbered scripts, one question each, writing figures/ and runs/
  tests/                pytest; tests/baseline: reference runs a refactor must reproduce
  figures/              charts in the report
  runs/                 result tables (*.csv), the sensor-placement cache and the trained
                        RL policy are committed; runs/saved (runs from runs.py),
                        runs/cache (operating points) and logs are not
```

Stages are numbered from 0 in the code, starting at the raffinate end.

## Python modules per phase

| Phase | Modules | Why these |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simulator | `casadi`, `numpy`, `scipy` | CasADi so the same equations feed the controller (decision 1). Its integrators handle stiff systems. |
| Disturbances | same, plus `matplotlib` | Just scenarios run through the simulator |
| Stage count, design | `casadi` with IPOPT | Solves the steady state directly instead of simulating 30 hours to get there |
| MPC | `casadi` with OSQP and qpOASES, `scipy` | A linear QP, built numerically each step and solved by OSQP through CasADi (decision 16), with qpOASES as the backup when OSQP fails (decision 30). A nonlinear `do-mpc` controller was tried first and is kept as a record. |
| RL | `gymnasium`, `stable-baselines3` (PPO), `torch` | The standard pair: gymnasium defines the environment, SB3 gives tested algorithms. Kept in a separate pixi environment (`pixi run -e rl`) so PyTorch doesn't weigh down the rest. |
| Workbench | `PyQt5`, `pyqtgraph` | Dockable, floating panels and fast live plots. pyqtgraph is pinned below 0.14, the last line that supports PyQt5. |
| Tests | `pytest` | |

All from conda-forge, managed by the shared `projects/pixi.toml`.

## Decisions

Each one: what, why, and what was given up.

### 1. The equations are written once, in CasADi, and used by everything

The simulator, the design optimizer, the controller, the estimator and the RL
environment all call the same `circuit.py` (with `chemistry.py` for the
distribution coefficients and densities).

**Why:** if the simulator and the controller each had their own copy of the
model, they'd drift apart and nobody could say which one was wrong. One copy
means any difference between "plant" and "controller model" is put there on
purpose.

**Given up:** CasADi expressions are a bit less natural to write than plain
numpy. Worth it.

### 2. The gap between plant and model is explicit and adjustable

The plant the controller drives is chosen by name (decision 24). There are
four:

- **matched:** the controller's own model. The reference, not a test.
- **perturbed:** the same code with a perturbed parameter set, drawn from a
  seed (decision 20).
- **settler** and **entrainment:** plants built with mechanisms the model
  doesn't have (decision 25, `plant_models.py`).

Upsets such as a flowmeter bias or a jackleg drift are separate. They're
scenarios applied to whichever plant is running (`scenarios.py`).

**Why:** Carester's point is that the gap between model and plant is where the
trouble lives. Making that gap something you can name and choose is what lets
MPC and RL be tested against it fairly.

### 3. Topology is data

`circuit.py` reads a connection map: stages are nodes, streams are edges,
section lengths are numbers. Changing from 18 stages to 60 is a change of
numbers, not code.

**Why:** the stage-count study needs it, and it's how a real plant changes too.

### 4. Every number has a source and a label

`parameters.toml` stores each value next to where it came from and whether it
was measured (from a paper), chosen (by me) or derived (computed from the
others). `APPENDIX_A_parameters.md` is generated from it.

**Why:** a chosen number is fine; a chosen number dressed as a measured one
isn't.

### 5. Time in hours, concentrations in mol/L, volumes in litres

Process time scales are hours (the Idaho circuit took 30 h to settle), so hours
keep the numbers readable. Flows are in L/h.

### 6. Four components

(La+Ce), Pr, Nd, (Sm and heavier). Enough for the Ce | Pr cut that makes the
NdPr product, for the Pr | Nd split used to check the model, and to show how
feed composition changes them. More elements is a change in `feeds.toml` and the
chemistry table, not a redesign.

### 7. A run is described in two places: the run file and the run spec

The **run file** (`configs/*.toml`) describes the circuit: stage counts, the
cut, the feed, flows, scrub, strip, saponification, targets, and which plant to
drive. `config.py` reads it, checks it and fills defaults. Chemistry and
geometry come from `params/parameters.toml`.

The **run spec** (`runs.RunSpec`, decision 24) picks what is done with it: the
plant, the controller, the upset, the sensor set, the length, and any edits to
the run file, the parameter file or the controller's settings. Saved runs keep
the whole spec.

**Why:** the studies are comparisons, such as two sensors against five, and a
comparison is only fair if the two runs differ in exactly what the spec says.
It also means any figure can be reproduced.

A run file can also carry `[parameter_edits]`: changes to the parameter file
for that run only, in the parameter file's own shape. That's how a plant with
other stage sizes gets its own run file (decision 28).

**Rule:** an option that is named but not built stops the run with "not built
yet" rather than silently doing something else. Today that is
`circuit.model = "exact"` and `saponification.mode = "full"`.

### 8. With a sensor set, the controller only sees readings

When a run has a sensor set, the controller gets readings through
`sensors.py`, with the noise, delay and sampling of a real instrument, and an
estimator turns them into a state. It acts on the handles listed in
`MPCSettings` (organic flow, scrub flow, scrub acidity, saponification, one
jackleg per settler), each with bounds and a rate limit.

Two cases see more, on purpose:

- **full_state**, the default sensor set, hands the controller the true state.
  It's the reference the sensor study degrades from.
- **The commissioning trim** (decision 21) runs with full information, the way
  a crew takes hand samples at every stage during start-up.

**Why:** that's what makes the sensor and actuator study mean anything: the
controller's performance changes only because of what it can see.

### 9. The stage model: a rate toward equilibrium

Each stage moves metal toward equilibrium at a rate (the "fast" model,
`circuit.model = "fast"`, the only one built). An exact-equilibrium stage is
the limit of the same equations as the rate constant goes to infinity.
Notebook 06 reaches it by raising the rate constant 10, 100 and 1000 times and
measures the difference in profiles and solve time. `circuit.model = "exact"`
is a named setting that isn't built.

## The model, in plain terms

### What one stage is

A mixer-settler. Two liquids meet in the mixer, metal moves between them,
they separate in the settler and leave in opposite directions. The model
keeps, for each stage:

- aqueous concentration of each component (4 numbers)
- organic concentration of each component (4 numbers)
- aqueous acid concentration (1 number)
- interface height in the settler (1 number)

### How metal moves (chemistry.py)

The extractant is an acid. It gives up three H⁺ to take one RE³⁺
(Carester eq. 1, Idaho Eq. 4). At equilibrium, for component *i*:

```text
c_org_i / c_aq_i = D_i = K_i · (free extractant)³ / (acid)ⁿ
```

- K_i is the only number that differs between components: fitted for Nd and
  Pr from the Idaho tables; Ce and Sm set relative to them (parameters.toml).
- Free extractant = total minus what the metal already holds. This is what
  makes a loaded organic selective: when it's nearly full, the component
  with the bigger K pushes the others out. That's what the scrub section
  lives on.
- Acid in the denominator: extracting metal releases acid, which stops
  further extraction. That's why plants pre-neutralize (saponify) the
  extractant, and why acid is tracked per stage.

### The stage equations (circuit.py)

Each phase in a stage is one well-mixed tank with a fixed hold-up (mixer plus
settler). The rate of metal into the organic is proportional to the distance
from equilibrium:

```text
r_i = k · κ_j · V_mix · (1 − φ_j) · (D_i · c_aq_i − c_org_i)
```

- φ_j is the aqueous share of the mixer's flow, so V_mix · (1 − φ_j) is the
  organic in the mixer.
- κ_j is a per-stage multiplier on the rate: 1 in the model, between 0.85 and
  1 in the perturbed plant.
- k = 380 /h, set so that a stage gets 95 % of the way to equilibrium at the
  Idaho lab's three-minute mixer residence time.

A stirred stage gets a fraction kτ/(1+kτ) of the way to equilibrium, where τ
is the mixer residence time, V_mix divided by the total flow through it. That
fraction is the stage efficiency. The mixer volume is the lab's scaled up
250 times, but the plant run files put more flow through it than that scale
implies, so τ is shorter than three minutes and the stages are less efficient
than 95 %:

| Run file | Extraction | Scrub | Strip |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ndpr_plant | 81 % | 85 % | 83 % |
| ndpr_small | 85 % | 89 % | 87 % |
| prnd_plant | 70 % | 73 % | 72 % |

Each mole transferred releases three moles of acid into the aqueous.
Balances per phase: in − out ± transfer.

### The interface (circuit.py)

Organic leaves over a fixed weir. Aqueous leaves through a jackleg. At rest,
the interface sits where the two liquid columns balance:

```text
z_rest = (ρ_aq · H_jackleg − ρ_org · H_weir) / (ρ_aq − ρ_org)
```

The interface relaxes to z_rest with a time constant (chosen, 6 min). The
densities come from the metal loading of each phase, so a change in feed or
flows moves the interface through the loading. The jackleg height is the
handle.

**Simplification, stated:** the interface doesn't feed back into the
concentration balances (hold-ups stay fixed). The coupling is one way:
separation → densities → interface. Enough for the controller to have to keep
it in its window. The entrainment plant (decision 25) is where the interface
position does change the separation.

### The circuit (circuit.py)

Three sections in a row, stages numbered from 0 at the raffinate end, with
n_e extraction stages, n_s scrub stages and N stages in all.

<!-- flowsheet figure: written by notebooks/11_diagrams.py -->
![the circuit's streams, where each enters and leaves](data:image/png;base64,)
<!-- end of flowsheet figure -->

The same figure as a file: `figures/diag_flowsheet.png`.

| Stream | Direction | In | Out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Organic | left to right, through all three sections | stage 0 | stage N−1, then stripped and sent back to stage 0 |
| Scrub liquor | right to left, through the scrub | stage n_e+n_s−1 (last scrub stage) | joins the feed at stage n_e−1 |
| Feed | right to left, through the extraction | stage n_e−1 (last extraction stage) | raffinate, out of stage 0 |
| Strip acid | right to left, through the strip only | stage N−1 | product, out of stage n_e+n_s (first strip stage) |

So there are two aqueous paths that never meet, scrub liquor plus feed down
to the raffinate and strip acid down to the product, and one organic loop
through both. With a reflux scrub (the NdPr run files), the scrub liquor is
part of the product sent back. This is the Idaho flowsheet layout (Figs. 17
and 21). The figure is drawn by `notebooks/11_diagrams.py`;
`figures/diag_circuit.png` is the same circuit with the ndpr_plant numbers.

`build_map(n_ext, n_scrub, n_strip)` writes this as a list of edges. The
simulator reads only the edges, so a hand-edited map (an extra feed point, a
side stream) runs without code changes.

### Saponification (setting `saponification.mode`)

- `simple` (the one built): the saponified fraction of the extractant
  neutralizes acid the moment it meets the aqueous. So it's equivalent to a
  NaOH dose, proportional to organic flow, carried along with the organic:
  spent where there's acid, and whatever finds none in a stage moves on to
  the next. A few lines in the acid balance, no extra state.
- `full`: track the sodium form of the extractant through the organic. Named,
  not built.

### The cut (setting `circuit.cut`)

The cut names the last component meant to leave with the aqueous. Everything
heavier goes to the product.

- `cut = "LaCe"` is the main case: La and Ce to the raffinate, Pr and Nd
  together to the product, which is NdPr. Sm and heavier are taken out
  upstream. Run files `ndpr_*`.
- `cut = "Pr"` is the Pr | Nd split, used only to check the model against the
  two published circuits. Run files `prnd_*`.

Purity and recovery in `metrics.py` are defined from the cut, in moles of
metal: purity is the product-side share of the metal in the product stream,
recovery the share of the product-side metal fed that leaves in the product.

## Decisions 10 to 35, from the model above

- **10.** **Rate model first.** Plain ODEs, and the Kremser check works on it.
    The exact-equilibrium limit is measured against it (decision 9), not built
    as a second model.
- **11.** **Hold-ups fixed, interface one-way coupled.** Stated above.
- **12.** **Saponification as an equivalent base dose.** Same acid balance,
    no extra state.
- **13.** **Cut is a setting.** One circuit model serves both splits.
- **14.** **Reflux scrub as a setting** (`scrub.metal = "reflux"`). The scrub
    liquor is strip product sent back, at an acidity the operator sets. Its
    metal is the product stage's own aqueous composition, read from the state
    (same trick as the organic recycle); the product flow reported is net of
    the reflux. An acid-only scrub on the 18-stage Pr | Nd circuit gave the
    textbook trade-off, 99.5 % purity at 4 % recovery or 95 % recovery at 75 %
    purity. Sending product back as scrub liquor, so metal displaces metal in
    the organic, is what plants (and the Idaho rig) use to get both.
- **15.** **Operating points come from an optimizer on the same model**
    (`design.py`, IPOPT with the model's own Jacobians). Two problems in a
    row: first the highest recovery possible at the design purity, then the
    least reagent that keeps recovery at or above a floor (the one given, or
    90 % of that maximum). Both respect the input bounds, the pump headroom
    (decision 19) and the loading cap (decision 22). A blind grid over flows
    found "best" points that were simply bad operation (scrub acid flooding a
    two-stage extraction section). The ECJTU patent has the same step under
    the name "steady-state optimization". Baselines are designed half a point
    above spec (99.5 % for a 99 % spec), as plants run, and
    `notebooks/02_design_baselines.py` regenerates the run files so their
    numbers are measured, never typed.
- **16.** **Two layers: a nonlinear steady-state optimizer and a linear MPC**
    (`mpc.py`). The optimizer (decision 15) sets the operating point. The
    MPC linearizes the circuit's own equations, discretizes them, and solves
    a QP each step: hold purity and recovery at or above their floors, keep
    every interface in its window, spend little reagent, move the handles
    gently. Measured feed composition is feedforward. This is how plant MPC is
    built, and what the ECJTU patent describes ("optimal set value through
    steady-state optimization", then predictive control on increments). The
    plant is a separate `simulate()` call with the upsets applied after the
    controller's handles are written in, so a flowmeter bias scales what was
    commanded and a hydraulic drift adds to the jackleg that was set.
    *Changed since:* the first version linearized once at the operating point
    and tracked targets. It now re-linearizes every step (decision 18) on its
    own model state (decision 21), and the targets are floors.
    *Record:* the first attempt was a nonlinear do-mpc controller
    (`mpc_nonlinear.py`): about 1.4 s per IPOPT iteration and no convergence
    in 200 iterations on the 18-stage circuit, so 90 s per step at best,
    out of the question for the 32-stage plant circuit. Kept for the numbers.
- **17.** **Sensors are data.** A sensor is a kind, a stage, a noise, a delay
    and a sample interval (`sensors.py`; the numbers are chosen and labelled
    in `parameters.toml [sensors]`). Two instruments are taken as given, not
    studied: the feed flowmeter and a pH probe on the scrub liquor line. The
    organic flow isn't measured independently: the controller commands it,
    and a meter that reads the command back is exactly why a flowmeter bias
    is invisible. An estimator (`estimator.py`) predicts with the nonlinear
    model on nominal parameters and corrects with a Kalman gain from the
    model linearized at the operating point and the sensor set's noise; a late
    reading is compared with the estimate at the time the sample was taken.
    A feed analyser, when present, is the controller's feedforward; without
    it the controller uses the estimator's feed estimate. With no sensors at
    all the estimator is a pure model run. Sensor placement (`07`) asks the
    model where an analyser pins product purity down best before any
    controller runs; the study (`08`) then removes sensors and handles one set
    at a time and scores the loss.
- **18.** **The estimator carries disturbance states; the MPC re-linearizes
    every step.** Two failures forced both. A plain Kalman filter made the
    estimate *worse* the more it trusted the readings: a 30 % feed change
    isn't white noise on every state, and a filter told so spreads the
    correction wrongly. With an offset on the feed composition and an offset
    on the organic flow as random-walk states (never more of them than the
    sensor set can resolve), the filter attributes a persistent surprise to
    the right cause, and hands the controller a feed estimate and a
    flowmeter-bias estimate it couldn't otherwise have. The MPC fixed at the
    operating point sent its moves the wrong way on a +20 % feed-strength
    step, whatever the tuning: an organic near capacity is too nonlinear for
    one linearization. It now re-linearizes every step (successive
    linearization); the QP is assembled numerically and solved by OSQP
    through CasADi's numeric interface, so a re-linearization is a Jacobian,
    a matrix exponential and some products, not a symbolic rebuild.
    *Changed since:* this decision linearized at the current estimate;
    decision 21 moved that to the controller's own model state.
- **18b.** **Hydraulic drift is feedforward too.** With the drift scenario the
    controller never touched the drifting settler's jackleg: its model said
    the interface would fall back by itself, because in the model the
    jackleg was where it had been commanded. A drift is a plant–model
    mismatch of the same kind as a flowmeter bias. Since an interface is
    measured and settles in minutes, the jackleg height the settler is
    really seeing follows from where the interface sits; the controller now
    infers that offset each step and plans with it. Excursion on the drift
    case: 0.365 → 0.006 m·h.
- **19.** **Design with pump headroom; the recovery floor is a price question.**
    The first plant baseline (on the Pr | Nd circuit, before the product
    became NdPr) sat at the organic pump's ceiling, so on a +20 % feed the
    controller couldn't add organic and doubled the scrub flow instead,
    losing purity. The design step now caps the organic at 85 % of a chosen
    pump maximum (4700 L/h, `[design]` in the parameter file), and the
    controller gets the full range. With that, the controller held 95 %
    recovery through the step (product metal lost 845 → 715 mol over 40 h) at
    33 % more reagent. Whether that trade is worth it is a price question
    (product metal against caustic and acid), and it's reported as one, not
    buried in a weight.
- **20.** **The plant is not the model (`mismatch.py`).** A controller that
    knows the plant exactly always looks good: the "inverse crime". The
    perturbed plant is built from a copy of the parameters, drawn from a seed
    and documented. Each extraction constant is multiplied by a random
    factor with a 10 % spread (20 % for the chosen La+Ce one); the acid
    exponent is 3.3 in the plant against 3.0 in the model; each stage's
    transfer rate is between 85 % and 100 % of nominal; the organic density
    has a 2 % spread, the salt's volume effect a 10 % spread and the mixer
    hold-up a 5 % spread. The perturbations are fixed for the run, not
    drifting. The controller, the estimator and the optimizer keep the
    nominal model. Reported numbers come from the perturbed plant; the
    matched plant stays available as the reference.
- **21.** **The model is never the plant: integral action and a commissioning
    trim.** The first run against the perturbed plant showed what a
    controller with no integral action does when its model is biased. Before
    the loading cap (decision 22), the plant sat at 98.9 % purity on the
    model's design handles (the model said 99.5 %); the model predicted the
    gap would close on its own; the controller cut organic, scrub and
    saponification to save reagent while purity fell to 96 %, and the loss
    over 20 h went from 156 mol (open loop) to 1042 mol. Three changes, all
    standard plant practice.
    (1) The controller keeps its own model state, run forward with the model
    under the inputs it applied, and linearizes there; what the plant or the
    estimator reports enters as an output bias (reported minus model purity,
    recovery and interfaces, filtered at 0.5 per step) added to every
    prediction. That's the integral action, the way DMC (dynamic matrix
    control, the first industrial MPC) and its descendants do it. The first
    attempt linearized the model at the plant's own state, and that's wrong in
    kind: a few percent away from the model's own steady states, its internal
    rates are large (|f| ~ 200 against 0 at rest), and its Jacobian there has
    a slowest mode 15× faster than the real circuit's and steady-state gains
    of the wrong size and sign (purity per +100 L/h organic: −0.13 on the
    model's own trajectory, +0.001 off it; recovery: +0.03 against +1.6). The
    same linearization, on the model's own trajectory, matches the full model
    to four decimals for single small moves over 12 h.
    (2) Commissioning ends with a trim: the controller runs on the real plant
    with full information until the product is on spec and the handles have
    stopped moving; where they end is the plant's operating point, and every
    scenario, open loop included, starts there
    (`commission.trim_under_control`). The extra reagent the trim needs is
    what the model's error costs, and the catalogue records it.
    (3) The handles the plan ends on must also hold the purity and recovery
    floors at steady state, as far as the linear model knows (its steady-state
    gain, with the drift included). The metal held up in a reflux circuit
    settles over days, longer than any horizon; without this the controller
    borrows from it: after a scrub cut the product rate read 160 % of the
    feed for hours while the recirculating metal drained, the horizon saw
    recovery holding, and the long run was a loss. With it came gentler rate
    limits (organic 50 L/h, scrub 10 L/h, scrub acid 0.05 M, saponification
    0.01 per half-hour step, chosen): the plant circuit's long-run purity
    moves about 13 points per 100 L/h of organic, and a model that's only
    roughly right shouldn't be trusted with big steps.
- **22.** **Loading margin in the design (`max_loading_fraction`, 0.85,
    chosen).** The reagent-minimizing optimizer loaded the organic to 95–99 %
    of its capacity in every extraction and scrub stage. D goes as the cube
    of the free extractant, so at that loading the model is very steep: the
    linearization from the perturbed plant's state predicted recovery at
    500 % and purity rising while the full model, from the same state, had
    purity falling to 91 % (plant and full model agreed to 0.005). A plant
    isn't run that close to saturation; the design now keeps every stage
    at or below 85 % of capacity, which costs organic flow and reagent and
    buys a model the controller can trust a few percent off the design.
    Every design-based result (stage counts, operating points, the
    catalogue) was regenerated with the cap.
- **23.** **Measure what you control; let an instrument say only what it
    knows.** With a perfect model, two analysers mid-cascade (the ECJTU
    layout) were enough: the model inferred the product from them. On the
    perturbed plant the first estimator reported purity 99.98 % and recovery
    92 % when the truth was 99.77 % and 95.2 %, the controller fixed a
    shortfall that wasn't there, and purity fell to 68 %. Five things,
    found one at a time.
    (1) An analyser reads every component the circuit carries (an XRF or ICP
    does); the Pr/Nd-only default was a leftover from the Pr | Nd case, and
    purity is about the impurity.
    (2) When there's an analyser on the product stream the controller takes
    purity (and, if the reading is prompt, recovery) from it as measured, the
    way DMC treats a measured controlled variable; the estimate stands in
    only for what isn't measured. A lab assay four hours old gives purity
    only.
    (3) The scrub liquor's acidity is read back: what the plant gets minus
    what was commanded is carried like the flow offset. Without it a strong
    scrub liquor had the controller pushing a handle the plant wasn't
    following, on the matched plant too (purity 47 %, 2240 mol lost); with
    it, 56 mol lost against 689 open loop.
    (4) The estimator's offsets have caps by kind: a feed offset 50 %, a flow
    offset 15 % (a flowmeter isn't 50 % wrong). With one cap of 50 % on both,
    the mid-cascade pair explained what a wrong model couldn't with an organic
    flow 850 L/h above what was commanded, and the loop crawled; with the
    feed cap at 100 % it fed the controller's model a doubled feed and
    saturated it. A feed that really doubles is what a feed analyser is for.
    The controller's model state moves by implicit Euler at a fixed cost:
    the adaptive integrator, on a model state fed by estimates, could crawl
    for minutes in its retry ladder after a pump stop, and a controller has
    to come back on time. The estimator keeps the adaptive integrator: its
    gain is built for the exact model, and where that gain is largest (one
    analyser late in the scrub) the cruder prediction was amplified into a
    15-point purity error where the adaptive integrator gives 5 thousandths.
    *Changed since:* decision 27 gives that adaptive prediction a budget,
    with implicit Euler as the fallback for a step that runs past it.
    (The RL environment uses the implicit-Euler estimator, for speed.) No
    reading's noise is taken below 1e-4 in its own units, or a component the
    feed doesn't carry puts a zero on the diagonal of R and the Riccati
    equation turns singular.
    (5) An interface reading is taken as the interface and nothing else:
    through the Kalman gain, a 2 mm reading against the model's tight density
    coupling rewrote the compositions.
    And what the controller is told is clipped to what a purity and a
    recovery can be (recovery at most 150 %, the bias within ±0.2 and
    ±0.5): the mid-cascade estimate on a stopped feed said recovery 2260 %
    and the QP planned on it. When a linearization comes out numerically
    useless (entries above 1e8), the controller holds its handles for that
    step and resets its model state to the model's rest point. With all of
    that in place, in the current study (after decision 30), the ECJTU pair
    holds the feed switch nearly as well as the product, raffinate and feed
    analysers do (41 mol lost against 931 open loop) but not a flowmeter bias
    (98.8 %, 290 mol off spec); the product and raffinate analysers see a feed
    switch late without a feed analyser (310 mol); a lab assay alone loses
    620. The placement study asks its question on the perturbed plant as
    well: on the model the best single analyser sits late in the scrub
    (stage 24 counted from 0, 0.10 thousandths); on the real plant the same
    curve sits forty times higher, about five thousandths anywhere from stage
    23 to the product stream (best 25 at 4.6, the model's choice 4.8, the
    product stream 5.8), the ECJTU pair 10.8, the lab assay alone 26. The
    real plant adds a floor no placement gets under, which is the model's
    error showing through.
- **24.** **Runs from a description; a front end that can be thrown away.**
    Everything a run depends on is one `RunSpec`: run file, plant, controller,
    upset, sensor set, length, and any edits to the run file, the parameter file
    or the controller's settings (nested dicts in the shape of what they edit).
    Plants, controllers and sensor sets are named entries in `registry.py`, each
    with a one-paragraph explanation; adding a plant is one entry. `runs.py`
    turns a spec into a session that steps one interval at a time (a generator,
    so a GUI can draw as it goes), a result (series, scorecard, settings) and a
    saved folder; the command line, the matrix and the GUI all go through it. The
    GUI follows the Passive-View MVP pattern (model, view, presenter): the
    presenter holds all the interaction logic and speaks plain Python to a
    `WorkbenchView` interface; the PyQt view only draws and forwards clicks;
    nothing that computes a number about the plant lives in either. Replacing
    PyQt with a web front end means rewriting `view.py` and `panels.py` only.
    The restructuring that made this possible (the closed loop as a stepping
    class, the controller split into named stages, commission-and-trim in one
    place) was checked against reference runs recorded before it started
    (`tests/baseline/`): bit for bit, every array.
    - **24a.** **The presenter touches no files (`src/store.py`).** Every file the
      workbench reads or writes goes through one module of plain functions: the run
      files and `parameters.toml` (as text, and saved after a check), where a setting
      is written and which code reads it, saved runs and their reports, and the
      session logs. The presenter passes names and gets back text, names and line
      numbers; it has no `Path` handling and no reads or writes of its own, so
      another front end can use the same functions. The log folder is defined there
      once (`workbench/logs.py` takes it from the store), and the five run choices
      are one tuple, `runs.CHOICES`. Found on the way: the historian could close
      before the server's last batch of tag changes arrived (they come once per
      publishing interval), so `Historian.close` now waits two intervals.
    - **24b.** **Level loops are part of the controller contract.** `loop.Controller`
      declares `level_loops` (the settler PI loops under the controller, or None when
      it moves the jacklegs itself), and every controller sets it when it's built:
      `HoldController`, `CircuitMPC` and `TwoPointController` take it as an optional
      argument, and the two wrappers (`FeedLossInterlock`, `DeploymentGuard`) take
      their inner controller's. The registry passes the loops in at construction
      instead of attaching them afterwards, and `ClosedLoop.step` reads the attribute
      instead of asking with `getattr`. Reference runs unchanged.
    - **24c.** **Every plant answers `hidden_at`.** `Circuit.hidden_at(x, t)` returns the
      state as it is; `DriftingCircuit` overrides it to set its slow drift, and
      `BookCircuit` inherits that. The closed loop calls it on every plant (unless the
      run turns drift off, as the commissioning trim does) instead of first asking
      `hasattr`. Reference runs unchanged.
    - **24d.** **No positions written as numbers.** Where the strip flow is tied to the
      scrub flow, the MPC wrote the inputs' entries 2 and 3 as numbers, in two places:
      setting the strip flow (`_u_full`) and adding the strip column onto the scrub
      column of the Jacobians (`_jacobians`). Both now take the positions from the
      inputs' layout (`self._lay["Q_scrub"]`, `self._lay["Q_strip"]`), as the lines
      around them already did for the scrub acid and the jacklegs. Same entries, so the
      reference runs are unchanged to the last bit.
    - **24e.** **One place builds the settler loops.** The registry built a
      `LevelLoops` from the stage geometry in two places, once from the operating
      point's jacklegs and once from a given model's (for the studies that rebuild the
      controller on a fitted model). Both now call `registry._settler_loops(rc,
      jacklegs, settings)`. `CircuitMPC` was left its size on purpose: splitting it
      waits until after the version is tagged.
- **25.** **Plants with physics the model doesn't have.** A plant built from
    the model's equations with other numbers still follows the model's laws, so
    it only tests the tuning. `plant_models.py` has two plants the controller's
    model can't describe, each from a flaw real mixer-settlers have:
    - **settler:** the metal moves between the phases in the mixer only, and the
      settler is three tanks in a row per phase that the liquid just flows
      through. The model lumps mixer and settler into one well-mixed pool. Same
      hold-up, same steady state (checked to 1e-15), different timing.
    - **entrainment:** each phase carries droplets of the other into the next
      stage, and they come back with their own phase, so some metal goes the
      wrong way. 500 ppm normally, rising to 2 % when an interface goes a few
      centimetres past its window. Both numbers are chosen.

    The plant's state starts with the model's layout (what leaves each stage,
    and the interfaces), and the rest is internal. Instruments and the
    controller only see the first part (`observable`), so sensors, metrics and
    commissioning work unchanged. In the matrix the full controller held all
    four upsets on both plants as well as on the matched one; on the pump
    stop it put nothing off spec on any of the four plants and lost at most
    27 mol of NdPr. That's one weight and one draw of each plant; the pump
    stop is fragile across both (decisions 26 and 29). The controller
    linearized once, with no output bias, did badly on every plant, the
    matched one included: 4,721 to 4,833 mol off spec on a feed switch.
    *Changed since:* the first matrix (Oct 9, before decision 26) had
    entrainment as the one cost on the pump stop (84 mol lost, the matched
    plant about zero) and the fixed controller three times worse on the new
    plants than on the matched one. Both moved when the centering term was
    fixed. After decision 26 the pump stop put 0 to 195 mol off spec across
    the plants, and the matched plant lost 1,300 mol of NdPr; after
    decision 30 (the solver backup) none of that is left at this weight. The
    matrix is one file from one run.
- **26.** **Interface centering, fixed (Oct 13).** The QP has a term that
    pulls each interface toward its setpoint (`w_center` = 0.02 per cm²), so
    after an upset the jacklegs bring interfaces back to the middle of their
    window, not just inside it. The code divided the offset in metres by 100
    where it should have multiplied, so the term was 10⁸ times weaker than
    meant and did nothing; every result before Oct 13 was made that way. Fixed
    in `mpc.py`. The commissioning trim uses the controller, so the trimmed
    operating point moved slightly (reagent 2,712 → 2,717 mol/h) and every
    result that starts from it moved a little: the 60 h open-loop catalogue,
    both 40 h catalogues and the commissioning tables, the sensor and handle
    study, the structural matrix and the learned policy (retrained). The
    stage-count sweeps, the design point and the sensor placement don't use
    the controller and didn't move.
    Then the weight was swept from 0 to 0.02 on six cases
    (`notebooks/15_center_weight_sweep.py`). The feed switch, the drift and the
    flowmeter bias come out about the same at every weight, the drift a little
    better with the pull. The pump stop jumps around with no pattern. As
    rerun after decision 30: the entrainment plant loses 1,233 mol of NdPr at
    0.0002 and 1,480 at 0.005, and at most 110 at the others; the matched
    plant puts 520 mol off spec at 0.005 and next to nothing at the others.
    So the controller's behaviour after a pump stop is fragile: small
    numerical differences decide whether it rides through or runs away. The
    cause: while the feed is off and the circuit refills, recovery reads
    nonsense and the controller acts on it. The earlier "nothing lost on the
    matched plant" was luck.
    *Changed since:* before decision 30 the sweep had the matched plant
    losing about 1,400 mol at 0 and 1,300 at 0.02, and the entrainment plant
    1,435 at 0.001. The numbers moved with the solver change; the fragility
    didn't go away.
    **Kept** at 0.02, and the pump stop is documented as a limit. The plant
    answer is an interlock (Open). Two simpler versions were tried on Oct 8
    and reverted, because each broke another upset: holding the handles while
    the feed is off, and recovery read against a filtered feed.
- **27.** **The estimator's prediction has a budget.** With the ECJTU pair,
    after decision 26, the estimator's adaptive integrator crawled on some
    estimates, millions of tiny steps for one half hour, and runs hung. The
    prediction now gets 20,000 evaluations of the model (chosen: a few hundred
    times what a normal step needs). Past that it falls back to implicit Euler
    for that step, a fixed cost and a little cruder, and the step is counted
    in `slow_predictions`. In the case that stalled, 4 of 80 steps fell back.
    Plant simulations have no budget. Same principle as the controller's
    fixed-cost model state in decision 23 (4): a controller has to come back
    on time.
- **28.** **Stages sized to the design flows, as a side study.** The mixer is
    the lab rig's scaled 250 times, 30 L, sized for 600 L/h; the ndpr_plant
    design puts up to 2,594 L/h through one, so its stages reach 81–85 % of
    equilibrium (table above). `params/edits_sized_stages.toml` gives 130 L
    mixers (three minutes at the largest design flow) and 520 L settlers (four
    times the mixer, the lab rig's ratio). With them stages reach 95–96 %. The
    redesigned 32-stage point (`configs/ndpr_plant_sized.toml`) needs less
    organic (1,634 against 1,755 L/h) and less reagent (2,172 against 2,308
    mol/h), still at the 85 % loading cap: the flows don't go back up, because
    loading is set by the mass balance and tank size only sets contact time.
    Best recovery at spec with 32 stages is 99.6 % against 99.0 %; 95 % needs
    about 19 stages instead of 24, close to the near-ideal 18. The plant is
    much more linear over one controller move (purity nonlinearity 8–24 %
    against 25–111 % across the four handles) and less sensitive, and about
    3.5 times slower (slowest time constant 1,381 h against 393 h), so a 40 h
    run sees less of each upset: uncontrolled, the feed switch loses 80 mol in
    40 h and 2,678 in 120 h; the controller about zero either way. On the
    bigger plant the pump stop costs nothing under the controller, and the
    flowmeter bias puts nothing off spec even uncontrolled (`notebooks/13_stage_sizing.py`,
    `runs/stage_sizing_ndpr.csv`).
    **Kept as a side study:** the main case stays the 30 L plant. What made
    it possible: a run file can now
    carry `[parameter_edits]` (`config.py`, decision 7), which notebooks 02 and
    04 write and read with `--parameter-edits`.
- **29.** **The catalogue on twenty perturbed plants.** Every result was on one
    draw of the perturbation, seed 1 (B.10 #1 in Appendix B). `notebooks/14_seed_spread.py`
    draws seeds 1 to 20, commissions and trims each the same way, and runs the
    eight upsets open loop and under the controller, 40 h, full state
    (`runs/seed_spread_ndpr_plant.csv`). Seed 1 reproduces the report's rows.
    Each plant's best recovery at 99.5 % purity, from the design optimizer
    told its true numbers, is in `runs/seed_oracle_ndpr_plant.csv`.
    Five of the twenty (seeds 3, 6, 13, 14, 17) can't reach 95 % recovery at
    spec with any handles (best 72–92 %). On those the commissioning trim ends
    far below spec (seed 3 at 49 % purity) and every run stays below it. As
    rerun after decision 30, the controller cuts the score (NdPr lost beyond
    nominal plus product off spec) by a quarter to a half on every upset
    there (medians 2,490–3,570 mol open loop, 1,560–2,700 controlled), better
    on 4 or 5 of the 5 each time, but it doesn't bring purity to spec within
    40 h. Decision 30 has why.
    On the 15 that can, scoring the same way, the controller beats open loop
    on the feed switch on 15 of 15 (median 931 → 0 mol), the feed acid 15,
    the stronger feed 14, the strong scrub acid 14 and the flowmeter bias 8
    (open loop puts nothing off spec on the other 7). On the pump stop it's
    better on 2 and worse on 5, worst 1,703 mol: fragile, as decision 26
    found. On the drift and the slow mixers the losses barely change; the
    drift's benefit is interfaces kept in (none out on all 15, against
    8–12 m·h open loop), which that score doesn't count.
    The sensor study, the structural matrix and the learned policy are still
    on seed 1.
    *Changed since:* this decision first read the five plants as the
    controller giving up purity, the spec, to hold recovery, because purity
    and recovery are both soft floors with fixed weights and nothing ranks
    the spec first, and named prioritized constraints as the fix. That was
    wrong. On those plants the controller was mostly frozen by false solver
    failures, and what's left after the fix is the model's gains, not the
    ranking (decision 30). That second reading was wrong too (decision 30,
    *Changed since*, and decision 31).
- **30.** **A backup solver; ranked constraints tried and left off (Oct 14,
    evening).** Two findings from the five seeded plants of decision 29.
    (1) The solver. The QP (OSQP through CasADi) often reported "primal
    infeasible inaccurate" on plants far off spec, where the slack costs run
    into the millions. That's a false alarm: every output constraint has a
    slack, so the QP always has a solution. On a failed solve the controller
    holds its handles, so on those plants it was mostly frozen; on seed 3
    every step of every run failed. OSQP also wasn't repeatable there: by
    default it retunes its step size on a schedule set by its own setup time.
    Fixed in `mpc.py` (`MPCSettings`): `adaptive_rho_interval` = 25, so the
    schedule is fixed, and `fallback_solver` = qpOASES (active set), which
    gets the same QP when OSQP fails, before the handles are held. Each step
    records which solver answered (`qp_solver`). Every closed-loop result
    was rerun on this code: the 60 h and 40 h catalogues, the single-upset
    figures, the sensor and handle study, the structural matrix, the learned
    policy, the stage-sizing study, the centering-weight sweep and the seed
    study. On the five plants 401 of 3,200 steps still fail, 298 of them on
    seed 17, where both solvers fail on most steps of four upsets.
    Results that moved with it: on seed 1 the pump stop now puts nothing off
    spec (it was 190 mol), and on the twenty plants the controller is better
    on it on 2 of 15 and worse on 5 (it was 1 and 7). The sensor and handle
    study changed in places: the ECJTU pair with a feed analyser now puts
    2,300 mol off spec on the feed switch; product and raffinate analysers
    without a feed analyser run away on the pump stop (1,720 mol off spec);
    saponification no longer makes the feed switch cheap. The learned policy,
    retrained, now holds purity on all five episodes.
    (2) Ranked constraints. Decision 29's first reading was that the
    controller traded purity for recovery because nothing ranks the spec
    first. Both forms were built and tried (`notebooks/16_ranked_constraints.py`,
    `runs/ranked_constraints_ndpr_plant.csv`), each also used for the
    commissioning trim, on seeds 1 and 2 through a feed switch and seeds 3
    and 13 with no upset, 40 h: a two-stage (lexicographic) QP that first
    finds the smallest spec shortfall the handles can reach and then caps it
    there (`MPCSettings.ranked`), and one QP with a straight-line "exact
    penalty" on falling below spec on top of the squared one
    (`MPCSettings.w_purity_floor_linear`, at 1000 and 100). Ranking doesn't
    fix it. The two-stage form made plants that can make spec worse: seed 1's
    trim ended at 99.48 %, short of the 99.5 % target, and seed 2 fell to
    62 % purity on the feed switch with 4,592 mol off spec, against 98.3 % and
    536 without it. On the hard plants it helped seed 13 (98.0 % purity at the
    end against 89.0 %) and hurt seed 3 (85 % against 96 %). The exact
    penalty changed little on seeds 1 and 2 and gave mixed results on 3 and
    13. No variant brought a hard plant to spec in 40 h. Both are kept as
    settings, **off** by default.
    What's left on the hard plants is the model's gains. On seed 3, +10 L/h
    of scrub flow, run out long: the model says purity +4.6 thousandths and
    recovery −9.7 points, the plant gives +64 thousandths and −1.5 points.
    Same sign for every handle, only the size is wrong, about fifteen times on
    purity. So the controller moves too timidly. The remedy is correcting the
    model's gains from plant data, the adaptive rung of the controller ladder
    (Open).
    *Changed since (decisions 31 to 34):* both readings of the five plants were
    wrong. They came from a generator that drew separation factors outside the
    published ranges, and no setting of the handles can make spec on them
    (notebook 17). The "fifteen times" compared the model and the plant at
    different operating points. The solver fix and the backup solver stand.
- **31.** **Plants drawn inside the published ranges (Oct 15).** The
    independent generator gave each extraction constant its own random factor,
    so the ratios between them, which are what the separation depends on,
    weren't held anywhere: five of twenty plants had separation factors no
    published circuit has. `src/mismatch.py` generator "ratios" draws the
    separation factors themselves, evenly inside the published ranges widened
    10 % each side (Pr/La+Ce 1.64 to 2.42, Nd/Pr 1.18 to 1.75, Sm/Nd 6 to 14),
    plus one factor that moves every constant together (0.9 to 1.1). The
    report's plant (seed 1, independent) is unchanged; the seed studies use
    "ratios". On those plants the hard ones are the plants that separate a
    little worse than the model (Pr/La+Ce 1.77 to 1.96 against 2.0).
- **32.** **Level loops under the MPC (Oct 16).** In the model the interface
    feeds nothing back into the chemistry (the hold-ups are fixed, decision
    11), so the jacklegs earn nothing as MPC handles. `loop.LevelLoops`: a PI
    loop per settler, every 1.5 minutes inside the control step, tuned by IMC
    on the jackleg's first-order response. Controllers `mpc_level_loops` (the
    MPC without jacklegs and with its interface terms off) and
    `open_loop_level_loops`. Measured on the report's plant and the entrainment
    and settler plants, eight upsets (notebook 20): the interfaces stay
    within 0.1 to 2 cm of setpoint against up to 17 cm with the MPC moving
    the jacklegs, and losses are equal or lower, lower on the entrainment
    plant where the interface matters (feed switch 86 against 215 mol). This
    is how plants are built: local level loops, the MPC above them.
- **33.** **An acidity floor in the MPC (Oct 16).** Saponifying the organic
    spends acid. The MPC had no limit on it, and on plants that needed more
    extraction it drove the extraction section to almost no acid (1e-7 mol/L,
    even slightly negative), where the extraction law isn't valid (fitted
    down to pH 3) and a plant would precipitate. Its linearization then blew
    up (entries of 1e9, positive eigenvalues) and it lost the plant. The pump
    stop's weakness is the same thing: with the feed off, no acid comes in.
    `MPCSettings.acid_floor` (mol/L, off by default): every extraction
    stage's aqueous acid is an output, held above the floor at the interface
    check steps with a slack in mmol/L. At 1e-3, the floor the design step
    uses, the MPC with the plant's true model brought all seven hard plants
    of the first plant to spec where it had lost three of them (notebook 21).
- **34.** **The main case: sized stages, run with margin (Oct 17).**
    `configs/ndpr_main.toml`. (1) Stages sized to the flow (130 L mixers,
    decision 28): stages at about 95 % of equilibrium make the plant's unknown
    stage efficiency matter much less; on the sized plant the MPC with the
    nominal model and the acidity floor brings every test plant to spec,
    including the seven that defeated it on the first plant. (2) Margin: the
    controller aims at 99.8 % purity and 97 % recovery. Retuned to the
    cheapest flows that meet the targets, every plant sits on its own edge
    again whatever the design (notebook 25), so margin is where the plant is
    run. Running at 99.8 / 97 makes the band of scrub flow that keeps the
    plant on spec about three times wider for about 15 % more reagent, and
    more stages make that margin cheaper (notebook 26). (3) The acidity floor
    and level loops (decisions 32, 33). (4) A 120 h commissioning trim: the
    sized plant is about 3.5 times slower, and 30 h left some plants below
    spec. Run files may now carry `[controller_settings]` (MPCSettings
    fields) and `[commissioning] trim_hours`. On twenty realistic plants
    (notebook 14) every plant starts on spec, and the controller is better
    than open loop on the feed switch on 17, the stronger feed on 18, the
    feed acid and the strong scrub acid on all 20. The pump stop is still the
    weakest upset.
- **35.** **A plant whose chemistry drifts (Oct 17).**
    `plant_models.DriftingCircuit`: the perturbed plant with every
    distribution coefficient multiplied by a slow drifting factor (all
    together by up to about 10 %, La+Ce against the rest by
    `[plant] drift_split`), sums of sine waves with periods of one to seven
    days. Hidden states after the model's layout hold the log-multipliers;
    the loop writes them each step (`hidden_at`), they relax to zero with a
    1e6 h time constant so a steady-state solve pins them, and they stay off
    during commissioning. `Circuit` has three no-op hooks for it
    (`_read_hidden`, `_hidden_rates`, `_distribution_multiplier`); the
    baseline check is unchanged. On the main case a drift of up to 10 % in
    the separation factor over a week puts no plant off spec, even
    uncontrolled (notebook 27): the margin absorbs it, and the day-scale part
    averages out in a plant that settles over hundreds of hours.

36. **The workbench edits the files too, not only the next run.** The
    settings tree always edited the next run's settings in memory. Now
    File > Save settings as a new run file writes them, edits included, to
    configs/<name>.toml (the parameter edits go in its [parameter_edits],
    the controller's in [controller_settings]); the new file becomes the run
    file. File > Edit ... as text opens the run file or parameters.toml in a
    File editor panel; Save checks the file loads before writing it and keeps
    the old one as .toml.bak. Right-click a setting for its line in its file,
    the lines in src/ that use its name, or the file opened in VS Code at
    that line (`code -g`). The file work is in src/config_files.py, with no
    Qt in it, so the presenter stays toolkit-free (decision 24). TOML is
    written by a small writer there rather than a new dependency. The
    operating-point cache already hashes the run file and params/, so a text
    edit can't pick up a stale commissioning.

37. **A guard between the controller and the plant (src/deployment.py).**
    Shadow, advisory and closed-loop modes; moves at most 2 % of the
    commissioned value per interval and 20 % in all (a review in advisory mode
    may move as far as the intervals it stands for); a watchdog that holds the
    handles after three failed solves or an exception and stays out until
    re-armed; a journal of every interval. It wraps the interlocked MPC, so
    the registry offers mpc_shadow, mpc_advisory and mpc_guarded. The limits
    are settings a plant would set in its management of change.

38. **CircuitMPC.resync(): re-arm from the measured feed.** Re-arming (the
    interlock, the guard) puts the model at its rest point for the handles
    held now, with no bias. The first version built the inputs from the
    operating point, which put the model on the design feed and, with reflux,
    the design strip flow; after a feed switch the next QP had no solution.
    resync() builds them with _u_full and the last measured disturbances, as
    every step does. Also: a qpOASES solver that fails is dropped and built
    again next time; reused, it failed every later solve. Reference runs
    unchanged.

39. **Model updates go through a registry (src/model_registry.py).** Each
    fit is a version with checks (step from the model in use, a number on its
    bound, the range of the separation factors decide; the residual is shown
    but doesn't decide, see notebook 37), a named reviewer's decision, and
    activation; the version in use before is kept for rollback, and every
    event is journalled to JSON.

40. **The loop splits at the instruments (loop.Observer, src/plant_server.py).**
    What turns readings into the controller's Observation moved out of
    ClosedLoop into Observer, which needs only numbers that could come over a
    network; reference runs unchanged. The plant side is an OPC UA server
    (asyncua) with the level loops and the strip-to-scrub tie, as a DCS has
    them; the controller side is a client running Observer and the
    controller. They step in lockstep so a run over OPC UA can be checked
    against the same run in one process; every value carries a source
    timestamp in plant time, so the historian (subscription to SQLite) files
    it where it belongs. Security mode None in the demo.

## Open

- **Pump-stop interlock.** The controller's behaviour after a pump stop is
  fragile (decision 26). What a plant does: when the feed flow drops below a
  threshold, freeze the handles; when it's back and has settled, reset the
  output bias and the controller's model state from the plant before handing
  control back. Not built. A plant usually has an installed spare feed pump,
  but the feed can also stop upstream (leach, feed tank, filter), for hours.
- **Estimating the plant's own numbers.** The separation factors and stage
  efficiency as slow states in the estimator, so the model follows the plant
  instead of correcting after it; tested on the drifting plant, with and
  without an optical profile across stages (the stage-to-stage ratio of Pr
  and Nd gives the separation factor times the flow ratio). Then flagging
  faults (crud, fouled probes) from the trend of what it estimates. Not
  built.
- **Solver failures far from the design point.** The nominal-model MPC had
  15 to 39 failed solves in 240 steps on the sized plant when started from
  the design flows (notebook 21); none in the main-case seed study. Not
  looked into.
- **Stage efficiency at plant flows.** The main case is now the sized plant
  (decision 34). The Pr | Nd plant at 70 % hasn't been resized; that is a
  likely part of why it needs more stages than the published circuit.
- **Instrument numbers.** The analysers, pH probes, density meters and lab
  assay in `parameters.toml [sensors]` are chosen, modelled on typical
  instruments, with no vendor data behind them. Worth a pass with real
  datasheets before any of the sensor-study numbers are quoted.
- **Acid exponent.** n = 3 is the law; the Idaho fit prefers 3.9–4.5 but
  that swings the separation factor more than the mixed-metal data allow.
  It's a setting; worth one run each way.
- **Acid floor and cap in D** (floor 1e-3 M, cap D ≤ 1e4, both chosen).
  Measured: the floor doesn't move the operating point at all (3e-4 to
  3e-3 M, `notebooks/10_*`); what the optimizer sat on there was its own pH 3
  lower bound on stage acidity. That was measured on the Pr | Nd plant before
  the loading cap; the NdPr design sits on the 85 % loading cap instead, and its
  most acid-poor stage is at 0.018 M (pH 1.7). The cap was added after a pump-stop run
  under control drove nearly empty stages to D ~ 1e6 and the integrator
  stalled; at D = 1e4 extraction is already complete, loaded stages sit at
  D ~ 1e2, and the plant baseline is unchanged to four figures.
- **Two-way interface coupling** (hold-ups that move with the interface) and
  **full saponification** (sodium form tracked): neither is built; only the
  second has a named setting.
- **Economics in the controller.** The recovery floor is held at any reagent
  cost; prices for NdPr, caustic and acid would turn that into a trade.
- **Equilibrium constants for PC88A per element.** Still to source.
